title: Grand Tour
summary: Visit the Sun and every planet, from Mercury to Neptune.

steps.title: The Sun
steps.text: Our journey starts at the Sun, a star about 109 times wider than Earth. Everything in the solar system is held in orbit by its gravity.
steps.text_scientist: A G2V star with a mean radius of 695,700 km and 99.86% of the solar system's mass. Planetary orbits here are computed from JPL Keplerian elements.

steps.title: Mercury
steps.text: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and completes an orbit in just 88 days. It is about 40% wider than our Moon.
steps.text_scientist: Semi-major axis 0.387 AU, eccentricity 0.206, period 87.97 days. A 3:2 spin-orbit resonance gives a solar day of about 176 Earth days.

steps.title: Venus
steps.text: Venus is wrapped in thick clouds that trap heat, making it the hottest planet. It spins backwards, so the Sun rises in the west.
steps.text_scientist: Semi-major axis 0.723 AU, period 224.7 days, retrograde sidereal rotation of 243 days, and a surface pressure of about 92 bar.

steps.title: Earth
steps.text: Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only world known to host life. Notice its blue oceans.
steps.text_scientist: Semi-major axis 1.000 AU, eccentricity 0.0167, obliquity 23.44 degrees. The elements used describe the Earth-Moon barycenter.

steps.title: The Moon
steps.text: The Moon circles Earth about once every 27 days. In this compressed view it is drawn much closer to Earth than it truly is.
steps.text_scientist: Semi-major axis 384,400 km, eccentricity 0.055, inclination 5.14 degrees, sidereal period 27.32 days. Tidal locking keeps its near side facing Earth.

steps.title: Mars
steps.text: Mars is a cold desert planet with giant volcanoes and deep canyons. Robots have been exploring its surface for decades.
steps.text_scientist: Semi-major axis 1.524 AU, eccentricity 0.093, period 687 days, and an obliquity of 25.2 degrees that gives Earth-like seasons of unequal length.

steps.title: Jupiter
steps.text: Jupiter is the giant of the solar system, more than 11 times wider than Earth. Its bands are storm clouds stretched out by its fast spin.
steps.text_scientist: Semi-major axis 5.203 AU, period 11.86 years, a mass of about 318 Earth masses, and a sidereal rotation period near 9.9 hours.

steps.title: Saturn
steps.text: Saturn is the second-largest planet and is known for its system of icy rings. It is so light for its size that it would float in water.
steps.text_scientist: Semi-major axis 9.537 AU, period 29.4 years, a mean density of about 0.69 g/cm3, and rings made mostly of water ice.

steps.title: Uranus
steps.text: Uranus is an ice giant that rotates on its side. Its pale blue-green color comes from methane in its atmosphere.
steps.text_scientist: Semi-major axis 19.19 AU, period 84 years, obliquity 97.8 degrees, and a retrograde rotation period of about 17.2 hours.

steps.title: Neptune
steps.text: Neptune is the most distant planet, about 30 times farther from the Sun than Earth. Sunlight takes over four hours to reach it.
steps.text_scientist: Semi-major axis 30.07 AU, period 164.8 years, and sustained winds above 2,000 km/h in its upper atmosphere.

title: Earth and Moon
summary: See how the Moon orbits Earth, and how far away it really is.

steps.title: A planet and its Moon
steps.text: Earth and the Moon form a pair. The Moon's gravity raises our ocean tides and helps keep Earth's tilt steady over very long times.
steps.text_scientist: The Moon has about 1.2% of Earth's mass, so the two bodies orbit a common barycenter that lies inside Earth, about 4,600 km from its center.

steps.title: Always the same face
steps.text: The Moon always shows Earth the same face. It takes about 27 days to orbit Earth, and the same time to spin once.
steps.text_scientist: Tidal locking synchronizes the sidereal rotation period with the 27.32-day orbital period. Orbital eccentricity of 0.055 causes visible libration.

steps.title: The true distance
steps.text: At true scale, the Moon is about 30 Earth-widths away. Distances in space are far larger than most models suggest.
steps.text_scientist: The mean Earth-Moon distance of 384,400 km is about 60 Earth radii, or 30 Earth diameters.

steps.title: A second away
steps.text: Light takes just over one second to travel from the Moon to Earth. Sunlight, by comparison, needs about eight minutes.
steps.text_scientist: At 384,400 km the one-way light time is about 1.28 s. At 1 AU the light time is about 499 s.

title: Sense of Scale
summary: Compare the true sizes and distances of Earth, Jupiter, the Sun, and Neptune.

steps.title: Earth
steps.text: This is Earth at true scale, 12,742 km across. Remember this size as we compare other worlds.
steps.text_scientist: Mean radius 6,371 km. All sizes and distances in true-scale mode are drawn at 1 render unit per 1,000 km.

steps.title: Jupiter
steps.text: Jupiter is about 11 times wider than Earth. More than 1,300 Earths could fit inside it.
steps.text_scientist: Mean radius 69,911 km, a volume ratio of about 1,321 Earths, and a mass of about 318 Earth masses.

steps.title: The Sun
steps.text: The Sun is about 109 times wider than Earth, and about 1.3 million Earths could fit inside it.
steps.text_scientist: Mean radius 695,700 km, a volume ratio of about 1.3 million Earths, and 99.86% of the solar system's mass.

steps.title: Neptune
steps.text: Neptune orbits about 4.5 billion kilometers from the Sun. Sunlight needs over four hours to reach it.
steps.text_scientist: Semi-major axis 30.07 AU, so the one-way light time from the Sun is about 4.2 hours.

title: Moons and Dwarf Planets
summary: Meet volcanic Io, ocean world Europa, giant Ganymede, hazy Titan, and the dwarf planets Ceres and Pluto.

steps.title: Io
steps.text: Io is the most volcanic world we know. Jupiter's gravity squeezes it on every orbit, and that heat feeds hundreds of active volcanoes.
steps.text_scientist: Io's forced eccentricity comes from the 1:2:4 Laplace resonance with Europa and Ganymede. Tidal dissipation yields a global heat flow of about 2 W/m2.

steps.title: Europa
steps.text: Under Europa's cracked ice lies a salty ocean with more water than all of Earth's oceans. It is one of the best places to search for life.
steps.text_scientist: Galileo measured an induced magnetic field that points to a conducting ocean beneath an ice shell roughly 15 to 25 km thick.

steps.title: Ganymede
steps.text: Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system, wider than the planet Mercury. It is the only moon with its own magnetic field.
steps.text_scientist: With a radius of 2,634 km and a normalized moment of inertia near 0.31, Ganymede has an iron core whose dynamo creates a small magnetosphere.

steps.title: Titan
steps.text: Titan, Saturn's biggest moon, has a thick orange sky. Rain made of methane fills its rivers, lakes, and seas.
steps.text_scientist: Titan's nitrogen atmosphere reaches about 1.5 bar at the surface, where 94 K temperatures let methane and ethane exist as liquids.

steps.title: Ceres
steps.text: Ceres is the biggest object in the asteroid belt and the closest dwarf planet to the Sun. Its bright spots are salt left behind by salty water.
steps.text_scientist: Dawn found sodium carbonate faculae in Occator crater, deposited from brine that reached the surface from below the crust.

steps.title: Pluto
steps.text: Pluto lives far beyond Neptune and takes 248 years to circle the Sun. Its heart-shaped plain is a giant field of frozen nitrogen.
steps.text_scientist: Pluto orbits in a 3:2 resonance with Neptune. Sputnik Planitia is a convecting nitrogen-ice glacier about 1,000 km across.
